Interest of Amicus Curiae1
The Institute for Justice (IJ) is a nonprofit, publicinterest law firm. We defend the foundations of a free
society by securing greater protection for individual
liberty. That includes Americans’ ability to obtain redress at law, as they have since the Founding, when
their rights are violated  by government officials ( be
they federal, state, or local). So we litigate federal accountability cases across the country, including two
recent cases before this Court.  See Martin v. United
States (24-362); Brownback v. King (19-546). And we
file amicus briefs in such cases before the Court. E.g.,
Egbert v. Boule, 2022 WL 296925 (Jan. 26, 2022);
Tanzin v. Tanvir, 2020 WL 774437 ( Feb. 12, 2020) ;
Hernandez v. Mesa, 2019 WL 3854459 (Aug. 9, 2019).
In Hernandez, we argued that Congress codified “a
robust enforcement of Bivens remedies.” 589 U.S. 93,
111 n.9 (2020)  (quoting IJ amicus brief) . But the
Court disagreed, holding  that Congress “ left Bivens
where it found it,” with no “license to” expand the doctrine to new facts. Ibid. That preservation has proved
quite narrow. See Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482
(2022). So  we focus on another path Congress  preserved. It’s the traditional state damages actions that
remedied federal employees’ constitutional violations
for the nation’s  first two centuries . See 28
U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A) (preserving “a civil action
against an employee of the Government *** which is
brought for a violation of the Constitution”).

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or  in
part. No person except amicus or its counsel made a mon etary
contribution to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2

Introduction
We submit this brief to help ensure a comprehensive reading of the Westfall Act.  In addition to preserving Bivens and Carlson actions (in their limited
spheres), we show how the Act also preserves more.
Namely, certain state-law damages actions.
Respondent correctly argues that  in addition to
preserving some scope of Bivens actions via the Westfall Act,  Congress ratified the Carlson  action he
brings, via the Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA) .
That specific ratification should be enough for him to
prevail. But we  recognize that the Court may not
agree, based on its current approach to implied causes
of action, or the factbound nature of the new -context
inquiry. And, in any event, the PLRA’s ratification of
Carlson can’t reach cases of federal abuse arising in
Americans’ homes, cars, or businesses—the recurring
spheres in which Bivens actions are now routinely
held unavailable in the lower courts.
So we highlight the availability of another  remedial path Congress has preserved: state-law damages
actions brought for constitutional violations. That’s
“the traditional way in which civil litigation addressed abusive conduct by federal officers.” Hernandez v. Mesa, 589 U.S. 93, 110 (2020). And it endures.
See 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A) (preserving “a civil action
against an employee of the Government *** which is
brought for a violation of the Constitution”).
That tradition draws on a common law, sustained
by state courts, that “is not immutable but flexible .”
Funk v. United States, 290 U.S. 371, 383 (1933).

3

Importantly, “the whole point of the common law as it
evolved through the centuries was to vindicate fundamental rights,” so it “usually supplies a sound remedy
when life, liberty, and property are taken.” Browder
v. City of Albuquerque, 787 F.3d 1076, 1083 (10th Cir.
2015) (Gorsuch, J., concurring). The question is
whether Congress took that remedy away for constitutional violations when it channeled ordinary tort
claims to the FTCA. It did not.
Without analyzing the statutory text, r espondent
and the Government posit  that Congress “extinguished the  traditional remedy *** for unconstitutional conduct.” Resp. Br. 34; see U.S. Br. 29. Not so.
Below, we examine the text. We show that when it
comes to state -law damages actions  brought for constitutional violations , state law’s remedial role  remains. The Court should say so.
When this Court recognizes limits on federal judicial “authority”—as it has for Bivens actions—it commonly notes that the availability of state law mea ns
pleas for redress  won’t “echo into a  void.” Rucho v.
Common Cause, 588 U.S. 684, 718– 720 (2019); see
Danforth v. Minnesota, 552 U.S. 264, 291 (2008) (state
law can remedy constitutional violations where “no
remedy will be provided in federal habeas courts”).
Americans seeking redress  for unconstitutional
harms to their persons and properties should be similarly reassured. The Westfall Act, properly understood, means they can be.

4

Summary of Argument
Kekai Watanabe alleges that a federal prison employee, Francis Nielsen, was deliberately indifferent
to his serious medical needs, causing significant physical harm. If a state prison employee or the employee
of a privately operated  federal prison  did the same
thing, Watanabe would have a cause of action against
him, via § 1983 or state tort, respectively. See Estelle
v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976); Minneci v. Pollard, 565
U.S. 118 (2012). The question is whether Nielsen’s
status as a federal employee means no cause of action
exists against him.
As we briefly address in part I , Watanabe correctly argues that the cause of action this Court established for such cases in Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S.
14 (1980), remains available, given Congress’s considered decision  to preserve it  (and define its parameters) via the PLRA, 42 U.S.C. 1997e. Resp. Br. 34–38.
But the Court’s “current approach to implied
causes of action ,” including the factbound nature of
the “new context” inquiry, might render Carlson unavailable. See Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482, 499 –500
(2022). Even assuming the viability of Carlson actions
thanks to the PLRA , the general approach to Bivens
actions regularly leaves a “remedial gap” in federal -
employee accountability  in the lower courts , especially after Egbert. Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003,
1013 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring).
Those “concerned with history and tradition may
worry about Egbert  shutting the door on Bivens
claims for money damages, given that Founding -era

5

evidence suggests that damages suits against federal
officers were expected to provide a meaningful mechanism for accountability.” Jennifer L. Mascott & R.
Trent McCotter, Egbert v. Boule: Federal Officer Suits
by Common Law , 2022 Cato Sup. Ct. Rev.  111, 128
(Mascott & McCotter, Federal Officer Suits by Common Law).2
In light of that tradition, the Court’s sunsetting of
the Bivens doctrine warrants an examination of “the
implications that follow” for federal -employee accountability. See Trump v. Slaughter, 146 S. Ct. 2283,
2311 (2026) (Gorsuch, J., concurring). To that end,
what we outline in part II is not an “innovation” akin
to what Bivens effected “in the latter half of the 20th
century,” but a historically rooted “return to form .”
See Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229,
268–269 (2026) (Gorsuch, J., concurring).
That form is the  cause of action  everyone agreed
could already be brought for  federal employees’ constitutional violations when Bivens was decided. It was
“an action in tort, under state law, in the state courts,”
with the constitutional violation meaning a federal -
authority defense “would be lost .” Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Fed. Bureau of Narcotics, 403
U.S. 388, 390 –391 (1971) (re counting the Government’s view of the action available to Bivens,  then
supplementing it).
When it comes to damages actions brought for constitutional violations, the state-law tradition endures.
Watanabe and the Government think otherwise

2 Published before Judge Mascott’s appointment to the Third
Circuit Court of Appeals.

6

(Resp. Br. 34; U.S. Br. 29 ), because the Westfall Act
makes “[t]he remedy against the United States provided by” the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) “exclusive of any other civil action or proceeding for money
damages by reason of the same subject matter against
the employee whose act or omission gave rise to the
claim.” 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(1).
But Watanabe and the Government don’t engage
with the text of the  Westfall Act’s next clause. The
Act’s remedial exclusivity “does not extend or apply to
a civil action against an employee of the Government
*** which is brought for a violation of the Constitution
of the United States.”  28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A)  (what
we call the constitutional saving clause) . Everyone
agrees that that clause preserves Bivens/Carlson actions (disagreements over their reach  notwithstanding). Yet, by its plain terms (“a civil action”), the
clause doesn’t only preserve Bivens/Carlson actions; it
also preserves state -law damages actions “ brought
for” constitutional violations. So, in deciding whether
Congress preserved Watanabe’s  federal Carlson action (it did), the Court should not accept his unnecessary, atextual concession about the limits of the constitutional saving clause as to state actions.
As one analysis put it, “i f Congress intended to
preserve only Bivens and its progeny, Congress could
have made that clear. When legislating, Congress can
and does cite specific cases by name. But Congress
chose not to, and the Court must implement the design Congress chose.” Thomas A. Koenig & Christopher D. Moore, Of State Remedies and Federal Rights
at 32 (2025 manuscript) (quotation marks and citations omitted), https://ssrn.com/abstract=4462807

7

(Koenig & Moore, Of State Remedies and Federal
Rights). Tellingly, Congress also chose not to limit the
clause to preserving only federal actions. See Texas v.
DHS, 123 F.4th 186, 200 (5th Cir. 2024) (“When Congress wants to add the qualifier ‘federal,’ it knows
how.”).
So Congress’s  design, “[t]aken on its own terms
and read in its historical context, *** counsels in favor
of reading [the] exception for civil actions brought for
federal constitutional violations to extend to state
civil actions brought for federal constitutional violations.” Koenig & Moore, Of State Remedies and Federal Rights 32–33. At least, the clause preserves such
state statutory actions, id. at 33 & n.270, known as
“converse-1983” statutes. See generally Akhil Reed
Amar, Using State Law to Protect Federal Constitutional Rights: Some Questions and Answers About
Converse-1983, 64 U. Colo. L. Rev. 159 (1993) (Amar,
Using State Law).
The only question, really, is whether the state actions preserved by the constitutional saving clause
must be statutory. Or, whether they can also continue
in their traditional tort form when brought for constitutional violations . Some favor the converse -1983-
only reading. See Koenig & Moore, Of State Remedies
and Federal Rights at 46–47.3 Others read the preservation to also include tort actions brought for constitutional violations. See Carlos M. Vazquez & Stephen
I. Vladeck, State Law, the Westfall Act, and the Nature

3 Accord Bivens, 403 U.S. at 424 (Burger, C.J., dissenting)
(“there is nothing to prevent a state from enacting a *** statutory scheme” for damages actions against federal employees).

8

of the Bivens Question , 161 U. Pa. L. Rev. 509, 570–
577 (2013).4
Judge Walker cautiously endorsed both the tortinclusive reading of the clause and the converse-1983
reading. See Buchanan, 71 F.4th at 1015– 1018 (concurring opinion). In recognizing some preservation of
state-law actions, he’s not alone. See Cross v. Buschman, 2024 WL 3292756, at *5 n.12 ( 3d Cir. July 3,
2024) (Matey, J., concurring) (citing Judge Walker’s
analysis); Henry v. Essex County, 113 F.4th 355, 364
n.7 (3d Cir. 2024) (Judge Porter declining  to join the
portion of the opinion that rejected the cognizability
of a converse-1983 action).
We show that the tort-inclusive reading is where
the text of the constitutional saving clause leads. The
statutory context eliminate s any doubt. And this
Court’s precedents support our re ading. Constitutional structure, meanwhile, poses no barrier. Finally, the traditional tort action we advocate could
reach Watanabe’s  claim. That matters, because his
case arose in a state with no converse-1983 statute.
Argument
I. Watanabe is right about Car lson and the
PLRA, but the Westfall Act preserves more
than just Bivens/Carlson actions.
Watanabe is right that Congress preserved his
Carlson action via the Westfall Act and the PLRA.

4 Accord Carlson, 446 U.S. at 42 (Rehnquist, J., dissenting)
(“Congress intended to leave this responsibility to state courts in
the application of their common law”).

9

But he’s wrong to posit (unnecessarily) that the Westfall Act “extinguished the traditional remedy of using
state common law to hold individual federal officers
liable in damages for unconstitutional conduct.” See
Resp. Br. 34. As we explain in part II, that’s exactly
what the Westfall Act’s constitutional saving cla use
did not extinguish.
Watanabe correctly argues that Congress ratified
his Carlson action. This Court held in McCarthy  v.
Madigan, 503 U.S. 140 (1992), that Carlson plaintiffs
didn’t need to exhaust administrative remedies. Congress could have responded by eliminating Carlson
actions or strictly limiting them to their facts . Instead, Congress imposed an exhaustion requirement
and a physical-injury requirement. See Resp. Br. 8–9.
The PLRA “legislation enacted subsequent to [ Carlson]” is Congress’s “implicit acknowledgment that
damages are available .” Franklin v. Gwinnett Cnty.
Pub. Schs., 503 U.S. 60, 78 (1992) ( Scalia, J., concurring in the judgment).
That said, the  current approach to the “new  context” inquiry might  mean Watanabe’s claim doesn’t
proceed, even if only for minor fact differences from
past cases. See Egbert, 596 U.S. at 503 (Gorsuch, J.,
concurring in the judgment) ( Bivens doctrine no
longer even reaches cases whose facts don’t “differ[]
meaningfully from those in Bivens itself”). And, beyond the context here, the state of the Bivens doctrine
means that Americans’ reliance “on the continued
force *** of Bivens in the search -and-seizure context
in which it arose” is , at best,  on shaky ground. Cf.
Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120, 134 (2017) ; see Malinowski v. United States, 2026 WL 1948181, at *2

10

(E.D. Ark. July 6, 2026) (“The precedent holds out
what almost always ends up being the false hope of a
successful Bivens action.”).
So, the PLRA’s ratification of Carlson actions notwithstanding, Americans face a significant “remedial
gap” in federal -employee accountability.  Buchanan,
71 F.4th at 1013 (Walker, J., concurring). Even when
federal officers engage in egregious violence or deprivations of liberty.5
Against that backdrop, the Government  invites
the Court to make  even Carlson actions “a null set.”
U.S. Br. 25. Watanabe r ightly seeks to head off that
strange outcome. But he concedes too much about the
scope of the Westfall Act’s constitutional saving
clause. He’s right that Congress’s decision to preserve
“a civil action *** brought for a violation of the Constitution,” 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A) , cannot be rendered meaningless. See Resp. Br. 29.  But he’s wrong

5 See, e.g., Logsdon v. U.S. Marshal Service, 91 F.4th 1352,
1356 (10th Cir. 2024) (no Bivens action where officers executing
arrest warrant “secretly approached [Logsdon] after dark,” one
“ran up behind him and kicked him in the face, rendering him
unconscious,” and “three officers then stomped on him for two
minutes”); Ahmed v. Weyker, 984 F.3d 564, 566 (8th Cir. 2020)
(no Bivens action where officer “fabricated facts, knowingly relayed false information, and withheld exculpatory facts, all with
the intention that the three women would continue to be detained for crimes for which she knew there was no *** arguable
probable cause,” resulting in “a minor” spending “just short of 25
months in federal custody” ) (cleaned up); Oliva v. Nivar, 973
F.3d 438, 440 (5th Cir. 2020) (no Bivens  action where veteran
entering VA hospital was “wrestled *** to the ground in a chokehold”); Malinowski, 2026 WL 1948181, at *2 n.7 (no Bivens action where pre-dawn raid resulted in a “widow who watched the
ATF shoot her husband in the head”).

11

to say that the only way to  avoid that is by limiting
the clause to Bivens/Carlson actions. See Resp. Br. 34.
As we show below, that clause does more. It also preserves state-law damages actions brought for constitutional violations.
II. The Westfall Act preserves state damages
actions brought for federal employees’
constitutional violations.
“In the context of suits against Government officials, damages have long been awarded as appropriate relief.” Tanzin  v. Tanvir, 592 U.S. 43, 49 (2020).
Bivens actions were once an extension  of that tradition. But with Bivens now scarcely, if ever, doing that
age-old remedial work , has Congress left open another route? Yes. The Westfall Act preserves  s tatelaw damages actions brought for constitutional violations. That’s “the traditional way in which civil litigation addressed abusive conduct by federal officers .”
Hernandez, 589 U.S. at 110. “So we might expect exceptionally clear language if Congress had wanted to
abrogate that regime. Instead, we find statutory text
tailored to preserve it.” Buchanan, 71 F.4th at 1017
(Walker, J., concurring).
Here, (A) we provide an overview of that tradition,
(B) we show how the Westfall Act preserves it, and (C)
we illustrate how that preservation translates to a
state-law action in Watanabe’s circumstances.

12

A. State damages actions have traditionally been brought for  federal employees’ constitutional violations.
“In America, both before and after the Revolution,
the civil trespass action tried to a jury flourished as
the obvious remedy against haughty customs officers,
tax collectors, constables, marshals, and the like.”
Akhil Reed Amar, Fourth Amendment First Principles, 107 Harv. L. Rev. 757, 786 (1994). Those tort actions didn’t exist in a vacuum. They were brought to
enforce the rights secured by the Constitution , typically the Fourth Amendment. Ibid. Indeed, they were
a primary method of constitutional enforcement  at
law. “Because officers who violated the Fourth
Amendment were traditionally considered trespassers, individuals subject t o unconstitutional searches
or seizures historically enforced their rights through
tort suits or self- help.” Utah v. Strieff, 579 U.S. 232,
237 (2016).  Federal employees were subject to precisely such “an action in tort, under state law, in the
state courts.” Bivens, 403 U.S. at 390.
That system of tort actions brought for federal employees’ constitutional violations was expected by the
Framers and realized in our courts.
1. The “public debates on ratification of the U.S.
Constitution [showed] that officer suits were understood as an available mechanism for government accountability that would remain available under the
constitutional system.” Mascott & McCotter, Federal
Officer Suits by Common Law at 131.

13

To start, it was a damages action brought against
the king’s messenger  that “every American statesman, during our revolutionary and formative period
as a nation, was undoubtedly familiar with,” and “considered *** as the true and ultimate expression of constitutional law.” Boyd v. United States, 116 U.S. 616,
626 (1886) (emphasis added) (discussing Entick v.
Carrington, 19 How. St. Tr. 1029 (C.P. 1765)).
No surprise, then, that John Marshall emphasized
the effectiveness of state-court damages actions to assure his fellow Virginians that federal officers’ abuses
would be redressed. If a federal officer “will go into a
poor man’s house and beat him, or abuse his family,”
the “injured man would trust to a tribunal in his
neighborhood. To such a tribunal he would apply for
redress, and get it.” 3 The Debates in the Several
State Conventions on the Adoption of the Federal
Constitution 554 (Jonathan Elliot ed., 2d  ed. 1836).
That assurance would hold even in the face of “a law
made to authorize” the abuse, and even if “the federal
court [would] protect” the  officer. Ibid. “There is no
clause in the Constitution which bars the individual
member injured, from applying to the State Courts to
give him redress.” Ibid. Same would go, of course, for
Marshall’s hypothetical poor man.
“That background may explain why the Bill of
Rights did not contain an express cause of action. The
Framers likely expected our newly guaranteed rights
to be secured by old common-law actions.” Buchanan,
71 F.4th at 1015 (Walker, J., concurring). Redressing
federal employees’ rights violations via state- court
damages actions  was woven into our constitutional
DNA.

14

2. And it wasn’t latent. It was expressed in “[t]he
structure of these cases ,” where a constitutional violation would defeat a federal-authority defense. Akhil
Reed Amar, Of Sovereignty and Federalism , 96 Yale
L.J. 1425, 1506–1507 (1987). That structure “is illustrative of the myriad ways in which constitutional
‘public law’ protections are intricately bound up
with—indeed, presuppose —a general backdrop of
‘private law’ protections defining primary rights of
personal property and bodily liberty.” Id. at 1507.
To be sure, traditional tort actions weren’t brought
as constitutional claims, à la Bivens. And it was typically enough that the defendant exceeded statutory
authority. E.g., Little v. Barreme, 6 U.S. (2 Cranch)
170, 178 (1804).6 But still, the Constitution supplied
the rule of decision where the plaintiff alleged “an unconstitutional act, even if authorized by statute.” Butz
v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 490 –491 & n.15 (1978).
That is, such cases were brought for constitutional violations, even if not as constitutional claims.
Take, for example, Mitchell v. Harmony, 54 U.S.
(13 How.) 115 (1851). It was “an action of trespass
brought *** to recover the value of certain property
taken by [the defendant] *** during the late war with

6 The parties  mistakenly posit that “federal officers were
generally immune from such tort suits, [and] that immunity dissolved if the challenged conduct violated the Constitution.” Resp.
Br. 5 (citing Pet. Br. 4– 5). There’s never been any such general
immunity, nor the need for a constitutional violation. See Martin
v. United States, 605 U.S. 395, 413 n.2 (2025). While the Westfall
Act now requires a constitutional violation to bring an individual-capacity action, that wasn’t always so. Negligence could suffice. E.g., Westfall v. Erwin, 484 U.S. 292, 293 –294, 300 (1988).
As could an ultra vires act. E.g., Little, 6 U.S. (2 Cranch) at 178.

15

Mexico.” Mitchell, 54 U.S. at 128 . Notably, the plaintiff argued th at trespass in expressly constitutional
terms, as recounted by th is Court: “Private property
cannot be taken for public use without compensation
and against the consent of the owner.” Id. at 126; see
also id. at 127 (plaintiff citing “Art. 4 and 5 of Amendments to Constitution”). What’s more, t he judge instructed the jury  that the case “must probably ultimately turn” on the question of “taking of the goods
by the public authorities for public use.” See id. at 139
(quoted in opinion of Daniel, J., dissenting). And this
Court grounded its analysis in the Constitution too,
explaining that because “the rights of private property are” so “securely guarded under the Constitution
and laws of the United States,” “therefore *** the instructions of the” lower court were correct on the public-use issue. Id. at 136 (majority opinion).
Merriam v. Mitchell, 13 Me. 439 (1836), is another
illustrative example. It was a state -court “action for
malicious prosecution *** against an agent of the Post
Office department.” Id. at 439. There too, the plaintiff
made his case in expressly constitutional terms:
“[W]here an innocent man has been arrested and imprisoned, who has given no occasion for suspicion by
his own misconduct, he has a remedy against [the person responsible.] *** The supreme law of the land, the
constitution of the United States, art. 4 of the amendmen[t]s, protects the citizens from unreasonable seizures of their persons, and forbids the arrest of any
one, but upon probable cause. If a man proceed to act
in such case on his own carelessness and negligence,
he is to suffer, and not the innocent victim of his folly
and negligence.” Id. at 453. The jury instructions,
again, sounded in that register. See id.  at 457 (“The

16

Judge instructed the jury, that there was, in point of
law, no probable cause [.]”). And the state high court
held that the jury could find malice “from the want of
probable cause.” Id. at 458.
Those examples illustrate how  tort actions have
always been brought for federal employees’ constitutional violations—indeed, expressly argued by plaintiffs as such. “This method of adjudicating constitutional claims made sense: many constitutional guarantees were tied to common law rights.” Koenig &
Moore, Of State Remedies and Federal Rights at 14.
That tradition endured into the 20th century. See
Wheeldin v. Wheeler, 373 U.S. 647, 652 (1963) (“When
it comes to suits for damages for abuse of power, federal officials are usually governed by local law.”).
Which is why no one disputed  that Webster Bivens
had, as always, “an action in tort, under state law, in
the state courts.” Bivens, 403 U.S. at 390. 7 After the
Court supplemented that remedy, Bivens actions took
center stage, but the traditional state actions continued their remedial work too. See Koenig & Moore, Of
State Remedies and Federal Rights at 15–16 (collecting cases). This Court, no stranger to such cases, “recognized the continuing viability of state-law tort suits
against federal officials as recently as” 1988, in Westfall v. Erwin. Hernandez, 589 U.S. at 110.


7 Then, as now, the federal employees could remove to federal court. 28 U.S.C. 1442(a). The forum would be come federal
but the cause of action would remain state.

17

B. The Westfall Act preserves the tradition of state damages actions brought
for federal employees’ constitutional
violations.
Congress responded to Westfall v. Erwin (a negligence case) by making the FTCA the exclusive remedy
for claims within that law’s remedial orbit. But Congress preserved individual-capacity actions “brought
for a violation of the Constitution.”  Relying on text,
context, precedent, and constitutional structure, we
show that that preservation includes state damages
actions brought for constitutional violations , akin to
those recounted in the history above.
1. Westfall was a “state-law tort suit” brought  “in
state court.” 484 U.S. 292, 293 (1988). It didn’t involve
a constitutional violation. It arose from a federal employee’s “negligence in performing official acts”  (improperly storing “bags of toxic soda ash ”). Id. at 293–
294. This Court held he was not immune from liability
unless his conduct was “discretionary in nature.” Id.
at 300. That narrow term of art meant federal employees would typically be personally responsible for garden-variety negligence.
In response to that negligence decision—and the
backend indemnification paperwork it would require8—Congress generally just funneled individual-

the Westfall Act, Congress made  the FTCA “remedy
against the United States *** exclusive of any other
civil action or proceeding for money damages by reason of the same subject matter against the employee
whose act or omission gave rise to the claim.” 28

But Congress didn’t channel all federal-employee
actions exclusively to the FTCA. The Act’s exclusivity
provision “does not extend or apply to a civil action
against an employee of the Government *** which is
brought for a violation of the Constitution of the
United States.” 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A) (the constitutional saving clause). Such Constitution-enforcing actions were, of course, not at issue in Westfall.
That constitutional saving clause, at a minimum,
“left Bivens where it found it.” Hernandez, 589 U.S. at
111 n.9. But it also preserves more. It preserves state
actions brought for constitutional violations—and not
just statutory actions, but also tort actions. “[R]eading
the exception as a good-for-Bivens-only rule is in tension with the statutory text and context.” Buchanan ,
71 F.4th at 1017 (Walker, J., concurring).
“We start with the text.” Thompson  v. United
States, 604 U.S. 408, 413 (2024).  “Statutory context
confirms” our reading. Id. at 415. This Court’s precedents “support[]” it too. Id. at 416. And constitutional
structure doesn’t say otherwise.

19

2. The text. The constitutional saving clause preserves “a civil action” that’s “brought for” a constitutional violation. The first question is whether “civil
action” includes state civil action. It does , because
Congress included no qualifiers. The second question
is whether “brought for” includes only statutory actions or also tort actions. It’s b oth. Because Congress
wrote “brought for” (not “brought under”), what matters is not the source of action , but only whether t he
plaintiff seeks redress for a constitutional violation.
a. In the constitutional saving clause, “civil action”
isn’t limited to Bivens actions, or federal actions. It
“includes state or common law *** claims.” Texas v.
DHS, 123 F.4th 186, 200 (5th Cir. 2024) (assessing
the scope of “action” as used in another federal statute). “When Congress wants to add the qualifier ‘federal,’ it knows how.” Ibid. Here, it didn’t. Let alone the
qualifier “ Bivens.” The Court “cannot rewrite” the
statute to insert either qualifier, “when Congress only
wrote ‘an action.’” Ibid.
That decision is particularly telling given the “presumption of consistent usage.” Koenig & Moore, Of
State Remedies and Federal Rights at 33. Th e Act’s
exclusivity claus e, immediately before the constitutional saving clause, also refers to “any other civil action.” 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(1). Undoubtedly, that use of
“civil action” includes state actions , because it’s exactly what the exclusivity clause responded to  (t he
state negligence claim in Westfall). “It’s only natural
that Congress would use the term [civil action] consistently in the subsequent paragraph—indeed, in the
subsequent sentence.” Koenig & Moore, Of State Remedies and Federal Right at 33. So, “civil action” in the

20

constitutional saving clause includes state civil actions, just like it does in the exclusivity clause.
b. In the constitutional saving clause, “brought for
a violation of the Constitution” includes,  as Judge
Walker suggested, a claim whose “ purpose is to remedy a constitutional violation.” Buchanan, 71 F.4th at
1016 (concurring opinion) . That can come in either
state-law form  (statutory or tort) . “For instance, a
state trespass suit could proceed if its goal was to remedy an unconstitutional search. That interpretation
arguably tracks the ordinary meaning of the phrase
‘brought for.’ Courts have long used it to describe the
goal of a suit, not the cause of action.” Ibid.  (citation
omitted). This boils down to Congress’s choice of the
phrase “brought for” instead of the familiar “brought
under.”
One might read “brought for a violation of the Constitution” as unmoored from traditional tort actions ,
and assume it reaches only statutory actions—those
where “a constitutional violation is part of the plaintiff’s cause of action.” See Buchanan, 71 F.4th at 1016
(Walker, J., concurring). But if Congress wanted to
impose that source-of-action limitation, it could have
eschewed brought for  and used “brought under,” a
phrase “of common legal parlance.” Pinares v. United
Techs. Corp., 973 F.3d 1254, 1260 (11th Cir. 2020).  A
“suit is brought under the law which supplies its
cause of action,” typically a statute. Ibid.
Congress didn’t use  that source-of-action limitation. It used a purpose -of-action phrase. “A ‘civil action . . . brought . . . for” a certain injury “is an action
brought for the purpose of remedying that injury.”

21

Hoever v. Marks, 993 F.3d 1353 (11th Cir. 2021) (en
banc). More broadly,  “whatever object follows the
word ‘for’ *** informs what the ‘action’ is brought to
accomplish.” Id. at 1358. In the constitutional saving
clause, that’s “a violation of the Constitution.” So, by
writing “brought for a violation of the Constitution,”
Congress chose not to limit the civil actions it preserved by the source of authority they’re brought under; instead, Congress tied preservation to the purpose for which an action is brought (for a constitutional violation), regardless of source.9
That choice wasn’t arbitrary. While certain cases
(involving constitutional violations) would satisfy the
constitutional saving clause’s  preservation, Westfall,
the case Congress responded to, would not, because it
was brought  only for negligence, not any purported
constitutional violation.
In short, “a civil action  *** which is brought for a
violation of the Constitution” includes state actions,
whether statutory or tort, brought for the purpose of
remedying constitutional violation s—not just those
for which a constitutional violation is an element of

instead of others equally available.
3. The context. Context confirms that the constitutional saving clause preserves both state statutory
and tort actions. Start with background legal conventions (the common-law tradition). Then, the statute’s
immediate context (responding to the negligence
claim in Westfall ). Followed by  facts on the ground
(tort actions). And finally, constitutional avoidance.
a. First, “[b]ackground legal conventions” support
the tort-inclusive reading of the constitutional saving
clause. See Learning Resources, Inc., 607 U.S. at 301
(Barrett, J., concurring) (citation omitted). Recall that
“the traditional way in which civil litigation addressed abusive conduct by federal officers was by
subjecting them to liability for common- law torts.”
Hernandez, 589 U.S. at 110 (emphasis added).  And
they weren’t brought in a vacuum . It was “through
tort suits” that “individuals subject to unconstitutional searches or seizures historically enforced their
rights.” Strieff, 579 U.S. at 237. That’s what everyone
agreed was available in Bivens. 403 U.S. at 390. I t’s
what skeptics of Bivens pointed to as the appropriate
remedy for federal-officer harms. Carlson, 446 U.S. at
42 (Rehnquist, J., dissenting) (“Congress intended to
leave this responsibility to state courts in the application of their common law”).  And it’s how plaintiffs in
the illustrative cases of Mitchell v. Harmony and Merriam v. Mitchell won their Constitution -enforcing
claims. Supra, 14–16.
So t ort actions wer e, when Congress passed the
Westfall Act,  fairly described as  brought for

23

“unconstitutional act[s]” when the facts called for it.
Butz, 438 U.S. at 490. And, “[f]or two centuries, state
courts have had jurisdiction over these damage
cases.” Amar, Using State Law at 165. Congress knew
all that. See Goodyear Atomic Corp. v. Miller, 486 U.S.
174, 185 (1988) (Congress is “knowledgeable about existing law pertinent to the legislation it enacts”). I f
Congress purported to preempt that “field which the
States have traditionally occupied,” Medtronic, Inc. v.
Lohr, 518 U.S. 470, 485 (1996) (citation omitted), it
wouldn’t make sense to do so by preserving what that
tradition encompassed: civil actions brought for constitutional violations. Buchanan, 71 F.4th at 1017
(Walker, J., concurring) (“[W]e find statutory text tailored to preserve it[.]”).
b. The “context from which the statute arose” also
supports the tort-inclusive reading of the constitutional saving clause . Fischer v. United States , 603
U.S. 480, 498 (2024) (citation omitted). The Westfall
Act responded to a state negligence case, not a constitutional violation. If Congress wanted to also preclude
state actions beyond that underlying context, it could
have said so. But it didn’t. It chose a broadly worded
exception to the exclusivity c lause, preserving what
was not at issue in Westfall: a Constitution-enforcing
action. Buchanan, 71 F.4th at 1017 (Walker, J., concurring) (“[T]he Westfall Act’s historical context provides no clear evidence that Congress wished to upset
the long tradition of using state tort actions to police
constitutional violations. *** Westfall did not concern
a suit brought for a constitutional violation. And Congress enacted an express exception to carve out such
suits.”).

24

c. Facts on the ground at the time also support the
tort-inclusive reading of the constitutional saving
clause. Unless compelled by the text, it would be
strange to read the clause as preserving state converse-1983 actions but not Constitution-enforcing tort
actions—because when Congress passed the statute ,
the tort tradition was well- known and in contemporary use,  while the converse- 1983 tradition was  at
best fledgling, limited at the time to  one state.  See
Mass. Gen. Laws Ann. ch. 12, § 11H–11I (1979).10 The
constitutional saving clause, then, is best read as preserving the ubiquitous version of what it described
(tort actions brought for constitutional violations), not
an untested version contingent on the future acts of
state legislatures.
That’s not to say that the converse-1983-inclusive
reading of the statute falls away . To the contrary, as
Chief Justice Burger anticipated, “there is [still] nothing to prevent a state from enacting a *** statutory
scheme” in the converse -1983 mold. See Bivens, 403
U.S. at 424 (dissenting opinion).  The constitutional
saving clause also preserves converse-1983 statutes,
as “language that broad  [a civil action brought for a
violation of the Constitution ] easily accommodates
both known and unknown causes of action.” Hui v.
Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799, 806 (2010).11

d. Finally, constitutional avoidance militates in favor of the tort -inclusive reading of the constitutional
saving clause.
Congress’s work shouldn’t be read to leave Americans with zero remedy at law when federal employees
violate their constitutional rights. That’s the very outcome the Framers assured their delegates would not
happen, and it raises  “serious constitutional concerns.” Byrd v. Lamb, 990 F.3d 879, 883–884 (5th Cir.
2021) (Willett, J., specially concurring). Indeed, it
would violate due process. See Poindexter  v. Greenhow, 114 U.S. 270, 303 (1885) (“No one would contend
that a law of a state, forbidding all redress by actions
at law for injuries to property, would be upheld in the
courts of the United States, for that would be to deprive one of his property without due process of law.”);
United States v. Lee, 106 U.S. 196, 220–221 (1882) (a
system in which “courts cannot give remedy when the
citizen has been deprived of his property by force”
would “sanction[] a tyranny which has no existence in
the monarchies of Europe, nor in any other government which has a just claim to well- regulated liberty
and the protection of personal rights”).
Rejecting the tort -inclusive reading of the constitutional saving clause risks precisely that. The FTCA,
where Congress channeled ordinary torts,  contains a
host of exceptions, including for  battery by non -lawenforcement officers and for detention of property by
law-enforcement officers. 28 U.S.C. 2680(c), (h). When
such an act amounts to a Fourth Amendment

rest assured that a traditional tort action brought for

dozens of states without  a converse -1983 statute,
Congress has left him with no  remedy at law for the

as our textual analysis has shown.
4. Precedent. Read out of context, some of this
Court’s cases suggest potential roadblocks to our tortinclusive reading of the constitutional saving clause.
On inspection, not so.
a. First, the Court said in January 2007 that the
Westfall Act “accords federal employees absolute immunity from common -law tort claims arising out of
acts they undertake in the course of their official duties.” Osborn v. Haley, 549 U.S. 225, 229. That would
seem to suggest that our tort-inclusive reading of the
constitutional saving clause is foreclosed. But , that
same term, in June 2007, the Court went on to explain
that a plaintiff still “had a civil remedy in damages for
trespass” against a federal official unconstitutionally
trespassing on the plaintiff’s property. Wilkie v. Robbins, 551 U.S. 537, 551. The Court doubled down, assuring that “there is no question that one was available to him if he could prove his allegations.” Ibid. And,
lest there be any doubt, the Court reasoned that those
trespass “torts by Government employees would be so
clearly actionable under the general law that it would

27

furnish only the weakest argument for recognizing a
generally available” Bivens action for them. Id. at 560.
So Wilkie’s description of the law is on all fours
with our reading of the  constitutional saving clause .
And Osborn’s and Wilkie’s descriptions are easily reconciled. A tort action tha t’s not “brought for a violation of the Constitution” (e.g., the negligence claim in
Westfall) is subject to the Westfall Act’s FTCA exclusivity clause; but a tort action that is  “brought for a
violation of the Constitution”  ( e.g., as described in
Wilkie) remains available against the employee. That
distinction is,  as we’ve shown,  true to the text and
context of the Westfall Act, “accords with Foundingera principles of officer accountability ,” and accounts
for the “remedial gap left by” the sunsetting of Bivens.
Buchanan, 71 F.4th at 1012–1013 (Walker, J., concurring).
b. For the same reasons, there ’s no cause for concern raised by the Court’s tendency to shorthand the
constitutional saving clause as the “Westfall Act’s explicit exception for Bivens claims.” See Hui, 559 U.S.
at 807. Certainly, the clause is partly that. But it’s not
only that, for all the  textual and contextual  reasons
discussed above. No wonder, then, that the Court has
more recently described the clause by its actual, openended terms, in a manner tracking the Osborn–Wilkie
distinction. It “foreclosed common -law claims for
damages against federal officials, *** but it left open
claims for constitutional violations.” Tanzin, 592 U.S.
at 49 (citation omitted); see Simmons v. Himmelreich,
578 U.S. 621, 628 n.4 (2016) (“There is an exception
to [the exclusivity] provision for suits alleging constitutional violations.”).

U.S. 160 (1991), changes none of that. Smith , like
Westfall, was a negligence case with no constitutional
violation alleged. I d. at 162. So the scope of the constitutional saving clause wasn’t at issue. The question
was whether the negligence claim, which couldn’t be
brought via the FTCA because it arose abroad, could
still be maintained against the employee. Ibid.
The Court said no, but it didn’t impact the analysis
we’ve put forth. As elsewhere, the Court shorthanded
the constitutional saving clause as “a Bivens action.”
Id. at 166. Then, it noted the Westfall Act’s additional
preservation of “an action under a federal statute that
authorizes recovery against a Government employee.”
Id. at 167;  see 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(B). Finally, i t
called those the “two exceptions”  to the exclusivity
clause and refused to recognize “a third exception.”
Smith, 499 U.S. at 167.
Smith did not purport to establish the full scope of
the constitutional saving clause, because  it wasn’t at
issue. And, as we’ve shown, the state-law actions preserved by t he clause are not  a third exception —
they’re just additional versions of the first exception
(unlike the negligence claim in Smith). See Blanche v.
Lau, 609 U.S. 1, 11 –12 (2026) (this Court’s prior underinclusive description of a statutory term, in dicta,
cannot overcome the actual text).12

5. Constitutional structure. The Constitution
imposes no obstacles to either converse- 1983 actions
or state tort actions against federal employees. To the
contrary, the constitutional design presupposes that
if Americans’ “rights are invaded by either” level of
government, “they can make use of the other as the
instrument of redress.” The Federalist No. 28  (Alexander Hamilton).
Federal employees have never had a free- floating
immunity from state law, as the Founding-era history
discussed above shows. And, beyond what preemptive
reach a federal statute might encompass, any immunity implicitly derived from Supremacy Clause principles has been limited to “state criminal prosecution,
not (as here) state tort liability.” Martin  v. United
States, 605 U.S. 395, 413 n.2 (2025).
Similarly, “structural constitutional law” doesn’t
generally bar tort actions against federal agents, “regardless of the source of the tort principles,” including

doesn’t need to be revisited to give appropriate effect  to the constitutional saving clause.

“state law.” Hencely v. Fluor Corp., 146 S. Ct. 1086,
1097–1099 & n.3 (2026).
Sovereign immunity, likewise, doesn’t reach individual-capacity claims. Keifer & Keifer v. Reconstruction Fin. Corp., 306 U.S. 381, 388 (1939) (“ [T]he government does not become the conduit of its immunity
in suits against its agents or instrumentalities merely
because they do its work.”). Nor does, generally, intergovernmental immunity. See Texas, 123 F.4th at 208
(Federal law “flatly forbids agents from accessing
‘dwellings’ to prevent illegal entries. Suppose agents
were nonetheless barging into dwellings in violation
of the statute. Would intergovernmental immunity
prevent a homeowner’s trespas s suit? Of course not.
And that would be true even if the agents argued the
suit sought to ‘control’ how they were carrying out
their duties.”).
So it’s no wonder that, “[i] n the context of suits
against Government officials, damages have long
been awarded as appropriate relief.” Tanzin, 592 U.S.
at 49. Including in state courts, via  state law. E.g.,
Merriam, 13 Me. 439; Westfall, 484 U.S. 292.
C. Claims like Watanabe’s fit the traditional mold.
We close with a proof of concept.  It’s simple.
Watanabe brought this case for a violation of his constitutional rights, via the Carlson cause of action. But
he could also have brought it, for that same constitutional purpose, via state tort law, as preserved by the
Westfall Act’s constitutional saving clause . The tort
law of Hawaii, where this case arose, recognizes

31

medical negligence claims by prisoners  (to say nothing of general medical negligence claims). See, e.g. ,
Persin v. State, 143 Haw. 283 (Ct. App. 2018). As
Watanabe recounts, such claims have historically
been available to prisoners. Resp. Br. 40–41. The only
additional requirement, now imposed by the constitutional saving clause, is that his claim be “brought for
a violation of the Constitution”—which it is. See id. at
39–40 (citing Estelle, 429 U.S. 97).  That’s similar to
how this has long worked. Accord Cross, 2024 WL
3292756, at *5 n.12  (Matey, J., concurring) (“at least
some Eighth Amendment claims may be actionable as
medical negligence claims”). It still can.13

“We shouldn’t be surprised that the common law
usually supplies a sound remedy when life, liberty,
and property are taken. After all, the whole point of
the common law as it evolved through the centuries
was to vindicate fundamental rights like these.”
Browder, 787 F.3d at 1083 (Gorsuch, J., concurring) .
The Court should let those actions do their traditional
work.
***
Historically, there’s been nothing unusual about
holding federal employees accountable  via damages.
Or doing so by common-law tort, in state court. Or relying on those mechanisms to vindicate constitutional
rights. Indeed, when Congress passed the Westfall
Act, it knew all of that was quite usual . If it wanted

to suddenly limit that storied tradition of individualcapacity damages actions to the novel Bivens action,
it could have said so. But it chose otherwise. After
channeling tort actions not brought for constitutional
violations exclusively to the FTCA, Congress made
sure that “a civil action *** brought for a violation of
the Constitution” remained available in its traditional form. 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A). Not “a Bivens action,” and not “a federal action,” but “a civil action.”
Not even “a statutory civil action,” but simply “a civil
action.” As long as it’s “brought for a violation of the
Constitution.” Respecting those choices means recognizing the continued availability of state damages actions for federal employees’ unconstitutional acts. By
doing so, the Court does not “fill any hiatus Congress
has left in this area.” Cf. Hernandez , 589 U.S. at 118
(Thomas, J., concurring) (citation omitted). Rather, it
exhibits “utmost deference to Congress’ preeminent
authority in this area.” Egbert, 596 U.S. at 492.

Conclusion
The Court should affirm  because Congress chose
not to disturb the availability of Watanabe’s Carlson
action. In any event, and especially if it reverses, the
Court should make clear that the nation’s traditional,
state-law default for vindicating constitutional rights
remains available and effective.
